title: Product Strategy
summary: For product strategy managers: sizing markets, competitive strategy, business cases, strategic bets and partnerships, and turning analysis into a decision.
tests: Whether your analysis is sound and honest about uncertainty, and whether you can turn it into a clear recommendation that leaders act on.

rounds.title: Market Sizing
rounds.focus: How big the opportunity is, with every assumption visible.

rounds.title: Competitive Strategy
rounds.focus: Where to play, and how competitors will respond.

rounds.title: Business Case
rounds.focus: Should we invest, and how much?

rounds.title: Strategic Bets
rounds.focus: Build, partner, acquire or wait — and the memo that decides it.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: When the analysis said something unwelcome.

questions.title: Software for independent veterinary clinics
questions.prompt: Estimate the annual market for practice-management software sold to independent veterinary clinics in one large country of your choice. Then say what share of it a new entrant could realistically win in five years.
hints: Size it bottom-up: number of clinics × spend per clinic.
Which assumption would change the answer most?
followups: Corporate clinic chains are buying independents quickly. How does that change the size?
How would you test your spend-per-clinic assumption cheaply?
criteria: Defines the market precisely (independent clinics, software subscriptions, geography).
Builds bottom-up with stated assumptions and their sources.
Cross-checks top-down.
Runs sensitivity on key assumptions.
Converts to a realistic obtainable share with reasoning.
outline: Define: independent clinics; practice-management software (scheduling, records, billing); annual subscription spend.
Bottom-up: clinics × share independent × software spend per clinic per year (by clinic size).
Top-down: total veterinary services revenue × typical software spend share.
Compare; reconcile differences.
Sensitivity: number of clinics, spend per clinic, consolidation rate.
Obtainable: switching rates, competitor strength, sales capacity → realistic share.
questions.reference:
I would define the market first: independent clinics (not corporate chains) buying practice-management software — scheduling, medical records, billing — measured as annual subscription spend.

Bottom-up: number of clinics in the country (from a professional association or business registry), the share that are independent, and annual software spend per clinic, which varies with size — a small clinic might pay a few hundred a month, a larger one more. Multiplying gives the market, with each assumption stated and sourced or reasoned. (In an interview, state round numbers and show the arithmetic; the method matters more than the figure.)

Top-down cross-check: total veterinary services revenue times a typical share spent on software. If the two disagree widely, I would find out why before going further.

The most sensitive assumption is usually spend per clinic, which I would test with ten clinic interviews or competitors’ public pricing. Consolidation matters: if chains are buying independents quickly, the independent market shrinks each year. A new entrant’s realistic share depends on how often clinics switch — practice software is sticky — so a few percent of the market in five years is a typical, defensible assumption.

questions.title: The platform giant enters
questions.prompt: You lead strategy at a specialist company that sells scheduling software to hair salons. A large general-purpose platform announces it will offer free scheduling to all small businesses. What should your company do?
hints: What do salons get from you that a free general tool will not give them?
Which of your customers are most at risk?
What will the giant do next, and what will it not do?
followups: Your board asks about cutting prices. Your view?
Should you partner with the giant?
What would tell you the strategy is failing?
criteria: Assesses the entrant's incentives and likely depth in your niche.
Identifies sources of advantage (vertical features, data, payments, community).
Segments customers by risk.
Chooses a strategy (deepen vertical value, bundle, partner) with reasons.
Defines signals to monitor.
outline: Entrant's incentive: scheduling as a hook for its core business; likely generic and broad.
Our advantage: salon-specific workflows (stylist chairs, product inventory, deposits), integrated payments, marketing to salon clients.
At-risk: small, simple salons using basic booking only.
Strategy: move up to bundles of salon operations; free tier for simple salons; integrate where helpful.
Price: avoid broad cuts; adjust the entry tier.
Signals: churn among small salons, new-customer win rate, feature parity moves.
questions.reference:
First, the giant’s incentive: free scheduling is a hook to bring small businesses into its main business, so it will be broad and generic, not deep for salons. That defines where we are vulnerable and where we are not.

Customers most at risk are small salons that only use basic booking. Customers least at risk use salon-specific features: managing stylists’ chairs, deposits for no-shows, product inventory, client marketing and integrated payments.

Strategy: deepen what a generic tool will not build — move from scheduling to running the salon — and bundle it. For the simplest salons, consider a free or very cheap entry tier so they do not leave, with a clear path to paid features. I would not cut prices across the board: that gives away margin from customers who are not at risk. An integration with the giant’s platform could make sense if it brings bookings without giving away the customer relationship.

Signals: churn among small salons, win rate for new customers, and whether the giant adds salon-specific features — the moment it does, we revisit.

questions.title: Should we build a mobile app?
questions.prompt: Your B2B web product has no mobile app. Sales says customers keep asking for one. Build the business case: should the company invest, and how much?
hints: What would customers do with a mobile app — and is it the same as the web product?
How does an app change revenue: new deals, retention, expansion?
What are the full costs, including maintenance?
followups: Your revenue estimate depends mostly on retention. How confident are you?
What is the cheapest way to test demand?
What would make you recommend a smaller investment?
criteria: Defines the decision and alternatives (native app, mobile web, partner).
Grounds value in customer use cases and data (mobile web usage, lost deals).
Models revenue and cost with ranges, including ongoing maintenance.
Calculates payback and sensitivity.
Recommends with conditions and a staged approach.
outline: Use cases: approvals, notifications, quick lookups on the go.
Evidence: mobile browser usage, deals citing mobile, churn reasons.
Alternatives: responsive web, lightweight app for top use cases, full app.
Model: revenue from won deals, reduced churn, expansion; costs: build, two platforms' maintenance, support.
Payback and sensitivity on retention effect.
Recommendation: staged — improve mobile web, then a focused app if usage proves demand.
questions.reference:
I would start with what customers want to do on a phone. In B2B products it is usually a few things: approve requests, get notified, look something up — not the full product. That suggests alternatives: improve the mobile web experience, build a focused app for those use cases, or build a full app.

Evidence: how much current usage already comes from mobile browsers, which deals were lost citing mobile, and whether churned customers mentioned it. Then a model with ranges: revenue from deals won, churn reduced and expansion, against costs — building, maintaining two platforms indefinitely, and support. Retention is usually the largest and least certain benefit, so I would show how the case changes if the retention effect is half what we hope.

My likely recommendation is staged: improve mobile web for the top use cases now (cheap, fast), measure usage and its link to retention, and fund a focused native app if usage proves demand. The decision rule — what usage would justify the app — is agreed before we start.

questions.title: Build, partner or acquire?
questions.prompt: Your accounting software company wants to offer payroll. You can build it, partner with a payroll provider, or acquire a small payroll company. Recommend an approach.
hints: How strategic is payroll for your customers and your business?
How fast do you need it, and what are the regulatory demands?
What could go wrong with each option?
followups: The acquisition target's technology is old. Does that kill the deal?
The partner wants to own the customer relationship. Acceptable?
What milestones would tell you the choice was right?
criteria: Defines strategic goal (retention, revenue, data advantage).
Compares options on time, cost, control, risk, regulatory burden.
Considers customer experience and data ownership.
Recommends with milestones and exit criteria.
Plans integration or partnership governance.
outline: Goal: keep customers in our ecosystem; new revenue; richer financial data.
Build: control and margin; slow; heavy compliance across jurisdictions.
Partner: fast; low cost; less control and margin; relationship risk.
Acquire: speed + capability; integration risk; price.
Recommendation (e.g. partner now with an embedded experience, option to acquire later).
Milestones: attach rate, retention effect, partner reliability.
questions.reference:
I would start with the goal. If payroll mainly keeps customers in our product and adds some revenue, speed and customer experience matter more than owning the technology. If payroll data becomes central to our product, control matters more.

Building gives control and margin but is slow: payroll means tax rules, filings and liability in every jurisdiction — a large, ongoing compliance burden. Partnering is fast and cheap but gives less margin and control, and the partner may want the customer relationship. Acquiring brings capability and a team quickly, but at a price, and integration can take longer than expected — old technology is not a deal-breaker if the compliance capability is strong, but it changes the price.

A common recommendation: partner now with an embedded experience in our product, where we keep the customer relationship and data access contractually; set milestones — attach rate, retention effect, partner reliability — and keep an acquisition option open if payroll proves strategic. I would not accept a partnership where the partner owns our customers.

questions.title: One page for the CEO
questions.prompt: You have finished a two-month analysis recommending that the company exit one of its three markets. The CEO has fifteen minutes and has championed that market in the past. How do you structure the memo and the meeting?
hints: Lead with the recommendation or the analysis?
Who should see it before the CEO?
How do you handle the CEO's past position?
followups: The CEO disagrees in the meeting. What do you do?
criteria: Leads with the recommendation and its main reason.
Shows logic in a few steps with key evidence.
Makes trade-offs and risks explicit, including what would change the view.
Pre-wires key stakeholders.
Handles disagreement respectfully with evidence.
outline: Memo: recommendation; three reasons; alternatives considered; risks and mitigations; what would change our mind.
Evidence: one chart per reason.
Pre-wire: CFO and the market's leader before the CEO.
Meeting: ask for decision or next step; listen to objections.
Appendix: model, sensitivity, customer and employee impact.
questions.reference:
I would write a one-page memo that starts with the recommendation: “Exit market C over 12 months.” Then three reasons, each with one piece of evidence — for example, growth below the other markets for three years, margins that do not cover the cost to serve, and no realistic path to a leading position. Then alternatives considered (invest more, partner, sell), risks of exiting and how to mitigate them, and what evidence would change the recommendation.

Before the meeting, I would brief the CFO and the leader of market C, so the CEO hears no surprises and the market leader’s concerns are addressed or included.

In the meeting, I would acknowledge why the market was attractive when the company entered — the CEO’s earlier judgement was reasonable then — and focus on what has changed. If the CEO disagrees, I would ask what evidence would persuade them and offer to test it, rather than argue. The appendix has the model, sensitivities and the plan for customers and employees.

questions.title: An unwelcome conclusion
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time your analysis led to a conclusion senior leaders did not want to hear.
hints: How confident were you, and how did you show it?
criteria: Honest analysis under pressure.
Clear, respectful communication.
Openness to being wrong.
Outcome described honestly.
Lesson.
outline: Context.
Finding.
How you presented it.
Reaction.
Outcome.
Lesson.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “Leadership expected my analysis to support expanding into a new region. The data showed customer acquisition costs there were twice our core market and payback took over three years. I presented the finding with the assumptions that drove it and a cheaper test: a three-month pilot. They chose the pilot; it confirmed the high costs and the expansion was postponed. I learned that offering a test is often better than asking leaders to accept a conclusion on trust.”
